The Trail of Ninety-Eight
Robert W. Service (1909) · from “The Trail of Ninety-Eight,” Part III, stanza 2

Each man worked like a demon, as prow to rudder we raced; The winds of the Wild cried "Hurry!" the voice of the waters, "Haste!" We hated those driving before us; we dreaded those pressing behind; We cursed the slow current that bore us; we prayed to the God of the wind.

3
✏️ Daily Oral Language
Study the model, then fix the sentence.
✅ Model
Mercedes fussed over the packing; the men from the next tent grinned.

Mercedes is a name, so it takes a capital letter. Two complete sentences that belong together can share a semicolon: each side could stand alone.

🔧 Fix this one
hal and charles had fourteen dogs one sled could not carry food for all of them
Rewrite it correctly.
🔍 Check my work

Hal and Charles had fourteen dogs; one sled could not carry food for all of them. Hal and Charles are names, so each takes a capital. The two halves are complete sentences that run together, and a semicolon mends the run-on. A period works too. The semicolon shows the two facts belong together.

1
🍎 At the Board with Professor Lovelore
Semicolons, colons, and pairs
Professor Lovelore At the board
1:05
An AI-generated character and voice.
Semicolon
Two complete sentences that belong together.
It ate away from beneath; the sun ate from above.
Swap in a period: both halves still stand.
Colon
After a complete sentence, a : points ahead to a list or an explanation.
Buck had one wish: the lead.
Helper word
A semicolon can bring one, with a comma after it.
however·alsotherefore·moreover
The ice still held; however, the sun was eating it from above.
Pairs
either…orneither…norboth…andnot only…but alsowhether…or
Two warnings
1. Both sides of a semicolon must stand alone.
2. London’s day: ; and and ; but. Today: one or the other.
2
✏️ Grammar: Learn the Labels
Step 1 of 4 this week: label four sentences.

Pick a label, then tap the part it belongs to. A label can be used more than once.

LabelWhat it doesExample
complete sentencea subject and a verb; it can stand aloneBuck took the lead.
semicolonjoins two complete sentences that belong togetherBuck took the lead; Spitz was gone.
coloncomes after a complete sentence and points aheadBuck had one wish: the lead.
listitems that follow a colon, set apart by commasa sled, a tent, and a stove
explanationwords after a colon that tell what the first part meansBuck had one wish: he wanted to lead.
conjunctive adverba helper word after a semicolon, with a comma after ithowever, also, therefore, moreover
pair, part 1 and part 2two words that travel together; both appeareither … or, neither … nor, not only … but also
Buck wanted the lead;François gave it to Sol-leks
Two new dogs joined the team at the Rink Rapids:Teek and Koona
The mail drivers worked the dogs hard;however,they fed them first every night
NeitherDavenorSol-leks cared who led the team.

🗝️ Five Questions for Any Source
The same five you used on Gage in Lesson 2.

  2. What does it claim? One sentence, in your own words.
  3. What does it rest on?
  4. Who was it written for?
  5. What does it leave out?

📖 Priya’s draft, a model
Priya
7th Grade Scholar · her claim about Buck

Claim: The North keeps Buck alive, but it destroys the fair and trusting dog he was at Judge Miller’s place.

Some readers might argue that the North does not destroy Buck at all, because it makes him a master. After Spitz is gone, Buck takes the lead, and François cries, “Nevaire such a dog as dat Buck!” (London, Ch. 4). It is true that Buck becomes a great lead dog. But look at how he does it. He drives Sol-leks back “in a fury,” and on the first night he punishes Joe until Joe begins “to whine for mercy” (London, Ch. 4). The dog at Judge Miller’s place never had to make another dog whine to be in charge.

In the end, the North gives Buck power, but it takes away the trust he started with. Being a strong leader is not the same as staying who you were.
